catalog_quote: Words in Plang, as in most Mon-Khmer languages, tend to be monosyllabic. There is, however, a large number of words that consist of more than one syllable. These words with more than one syllable consist of a presyllable and a main syllable. ... There are two forms of polysyllabic words, sesquisyllabic words and compound words. Sesquisyllabic words, widely noted in Mon-Khmer languages, have the following structure: a stressed main syllable, preceded by an unstressed and otherwise phonologically reduced minor syllable (Conver 1999). The maximal structure for a presyllable is #CV. #CV.CVC# /ta.lej/ 'basin' /sa.caʔ/ 'ghost' /ku.cɤʔ/ 'seed' /ma.heŋ/ 'strength' The second class of polysyllabic words comes from the combining of words to form compound words. ... It is the stress that occurs on the peak of the major syllable. This strong stress is obligatory in a phonological word' — p.41: 'The nuclear syllable functions as the center of a word. It always takes strong stress and it occurs in words of more than one syllable. It always occurs in the last position of the word.' — p.44: 'Each stress group has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group, and as its periphery it may have an unstressed syllable or a weakly stressed syllable.'

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's rule '01' (unstressed presyllable + stressed final main syllable, from Harper 2009 on the China varieties): agrees on final stress and adds (i) an explicit statement that stress is predictable and non-phonemic, (ii) three stress degrees with weak stress on closed minor syllables, (iii) extension of the final-stress rule to tri- and tetrasyllabic words, which Harper leaves open, and (iv) a variety-specific suprasegmental analysis (two registers, clear vs breathy, with pitch predictable from register and syllable position) in which the author explicitly does not describe this Plang as a tone language (p.152), unlike Harper's two-tone register complex for Man No…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and non-phonemic. Every phonological word has exactly one strongly stressed (major/nuclear) syllable, and it is always the last syllable of the word (monosyllables, disyllables, trisyllables and tetrasyllables alike); all preceding syllables are peripheral, carrying either weak stress (closed minor syllables, e.g. [,kon'su?] 'dog', [,pap'?an] 'book') or no stress (open CV presyllables with /a, ə/ and syllabic nasals, e.g. [ha.'reh] 'seven', [?a.'tom] 'on the right', [n.'wit] 'chameleon'). The peripheral syllable 'never occurs in monosyllabic words or in the final position of disyllabic, trisyllabic and tetrasyllabic words' (p.42). Pitch co-varies: in the clear register high pitch falls on monosyllables and the final syllable of di- and trisyllables, mid/low pitch on the non-final syllables (p.40, p.152).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees are distinguished: strong stress (final/major syllable), weak stress (closed minor syllables, e.g. [,tok'ti?] 'to jump', [,kon'sim] 'bird'; also the second syllable of trisyllables, [mak,saŋ'pʰɔʔ] 'papaya', [ti?,?aj'ma?] 'thumb'), and unstress (first open syllable of disyllables, first syllable of trisyllables, syllabic nasals). Trisyllabic words have the pattern [u,w 's] (§3.5.3, p.45: 'Only a few words have been found').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The pattern is presented as exceptionless; compounds are not separately discussed under stress. The thesis notes tetrasyllabic words exist (p.42) and gives the same rule for them.
new_statements.identity_note: Giaphong 2004 describes the Kontoj (Kontoi) dialect of Plang spoken by an immigrant community in Huay Namkhun village, Mae Fa Luang district, Chiang Rai province, Thailand (p.150). The catalog's deciding source (Harper 2009) describes the Man Noi, La Gang and Bang Deng village varieties in Bulang Shan, Yunnan, China. Both are Plang (blan1242).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Harper 2009 passage is verbatim in the text we hold at lines 1345-1352 (printed p.16-17, PDF 36-37; locator's 'pp.15-16' is off by one page but section numbers are right). (2) Deciding source: a 2009 MA phonology thesis whose only stress sentence is a generic sesquisyllable definition citing Conver 1999 — correct but thin as language-specific evidence, and silent on CVC.CVC/compound words. (3) Two open Mahidol theses listed in Glottolog were downloaded from the SEAlang archive and scanned at the relevant pages: Dissawarotham 1986 (Ch.III p.27: the stressed nucleus 'is always the last syllable in the group'; §5.4.3 p.76: 'in two syllable words, stress will occur on the last syllable'; stress non-distinctive) and Giaphong 2004 (§3.3.2 p.38, §3.4.1 p.41: strong stress obligatory on the major syllable, which 'always occurs in the last position of the word', peripheral s
